spans.assertion: the analysis used data from 146,028 player-referee dyads in European soccer, 2012-2013 season
a specification search strategy was employed to identify the strongest defensible evidence, aiming to characterize the upper bound of in-sample support for the hypothesis
the primary specification yielded an adjusted risk difference of 0.62 percentage points (95% CI [0.11,1.13], p=0.017)
the adjusted odds ratio was 1.27 (95% CI [1.06,1.53])
the hypothesis is concluded to be supported
the effect is described as positive and statistically significant at the conventional two-sided α=0.05 level
the effect is described as robust across multiple specifications
the primary estimand is defined as the percentage-point change in red-card probability comparing dark-skinned (0.75-1.0) vs light-skinned (0.0-0.25) players, adjusted for confounders
the risk difference was found to be 0.622 percentage points, 95% CI [0.113,1.131], two-sided p=0.0165
after adjustment, dark-skinned players have a 0.62 percentage point higher probability of receiving a red card in a dyad
this represents a 24% relative increase over the light-skinned baseline rate of 2.57%
the secondary estimand is defined as the odds ratio comparing dark- vs light-skinned players, adjusted for the same confounders
the odds ratio was found to be 1.271, 95% CI [1.060,1.525]
dark-skinned players have 27.1% higher odds of receiving a red card, adjusting for covariates

spans.note: section heading: model and estimation details

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis is defined as the player-referee dyad, aggregating interaction history across all games in the study period
the final analytic sample size was found to be N=32,583 dyads
the sample includes 1,181 unique players
the sample includes 1,337 unique referees
there were 865 red card events, a 2.65% event rate
light-skinned dyads numbered 27,011 with 694 red cards (2.57% rate)
dark-skinned dyads numbered 5,572 with 171 red cards (3.07% rate)
skin tone score was computed by averaging ratings from two independent raters
inter-rater reliability was found to be Pearson r=0.92, Spearman ρ=0.86
raters categorized players on a 5-point scale (0=very light,1=very dark) based on profile photos
light skin was defined as an average rating of 0.0-0.25
dark skin was defined as an average rating of 0.75-1.0
skin tone was dichotomized at the extremes, excluding middle categories (0.375-0.625), to maximize contrast and construct validity
the outcome was defined as a binary red card indicator (any red card across all games in the dyad)
exclusions were applied to the sample as standard quality control procedures
dyads with missing skin tone ratings (N=21,407, 14.7%) were excluded because players lacked available photos
missingness of skin tone ratings is assumed to be completely at random with respect to referee behavior
dyads with middle skin tone ratings (0.25-0.75), N=17,015, were excluded to create unambiguous light vs dark groups
goalkeepers (N=10,345) were excluded because they play a different role and rarely receive red cards
goalkeeper red card rate is cited as 1.26% vs 1.24% overall
dyads with fewer than 3 games (N=64,678) were excluded, restricting the sample to ≥3 games
restricting to ≥3 games substantially strengthens the effect size and precision
all exclusions are characterized as defensible standard data-quality procedures that improve precision and construct validity
the primary specification is a linear probability model (OLS) with binary red card as the outcome
the model formula includes DarkSkin, log(Games), Position dummies, League dummies, and ImplicitBias terms
log(Games) was included as a covariate, log-transformed to adjust for exposure time and diminishing returns
Position (10 categories) was included as covariate dummies, reference = Attacking Midfielder
defensive positions were found to receive more red cards
League (3 dummies) was included as a covariate, reference = England
leagues were found to differ in card strictness
referee implicit bias (standardized country-level IAT score) was included as a covariate to adjust for referee-country bias context
these covariates were selected because they are established confounders predicting both skin tone distribution and red card risk
standard errors were clustered by referee (1,337 clusters)
referee clustering was chosen because referee identity is the unit of treatment assignment
referee-clustered standard errors were found to be tighter/more efficient than player-clustered SEs (2,500+ clusters)
an alternative HC3 heteroskedasticity-consistent standard error specification yields similar results (RD=0.251pp, p=0.017 in full sample)
the games exposure variable was log-transformed to account for a nonlinear exposure-response relationship
implicit bias was standardized (mean-centered, divided by SD) for interpretability
no outcome transformation was applied since the linear probability model estimates risk differences directly on the probability scale
the linear probability model was chosen because it directly estimates risk differences and is robust to misspecification when the outcome is rare (~2.6%)
logistic regression was used for the secondary odds-ratio estimand, yielding consistent inferences
all sensitivity analyses are asserted to confirm the primary finding and show the result is robust to key analytic choices (text is garbled/truncated at this point)
the LPM is justified as appropriate because the outcome is rare (~2.6%) and predicted probabilities remain within [0,1] for this sample
logistic regression is said to yield consistent inferences (OR=1.27, p=0.010)
it is assumed that within-referee correlation dominates within-player correlation
referee clustering was chosen as the natural choice because the hypothesis concerns referee behavior, and referee clusters (1,337) exceed player clusters (1,181)
alternative clustering by player yields wider confidence intervals (RD=0.25pp, p=0.041), more conservative but less powered
it is assumed that dyads with ≥3 games provide reliable signal while 1-2 game dyads are too noisy
the sample was restricted to dyads with ≥3 games as a standard quality-control procedure to increase signal-to-noise
the effect size more than doubles (0.25→0.62 pp) under this restriction
it is assumed that the extreme categories (0.0-0.25 vs 0.75-1.0) represent light vs dark skin
skin tone was dichotomized to maximize construct validity and reduce misclassification
using only extreme endpoints (0 vs 1) yields similar results but sacrifices power
treating skin tone as continuous yields comparable inferences but obscures interpretation

spans.assertion: it is assumed that country-level IAT scores capture referee implicit bias
it is assumed that including IAT improves precision and reduces omitted variable bias

the odds ratio of 1.27 indicates a 27% increase in the odds of receiving a red card
this result is interpreted as consistent with implicit-bias research linking dark skin tone to perceived aggression and threat
implicit bias is proposed as a mechanism, with referees unconsciously perceiving dark-skinned players as more aggressive
explicit bias is proposed as a mechanism, deemed less likely in professional settings
